artworks.title: Lucanian red-figure nestoris: Melampus healing the daughters of Proetus
artworks.description: A Lucanian red-figure nestoris of about 360 BC, now in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples, carries one of the rare ancient images of the seer Melampus at work. The scene is set in a sanctuary: Melampus stands ministering while a seated priestess attends, and the two stricken daughters of King Proetus — driven mad and roaming the hills — are gathered for their cure. Artemis appears at the center with Dionysus and a satyr rendered in pale added color, framing the rite as a divine purification. It is the visual counterpart to the myth in which Melampus, son of Amythaon, healed the Proetids of their frenzy in return for a share of the Argive kingdom, and it remains a key witness to how South Italian painters imagined the prophet-healer in action.

artworks.title: Melampus and the Centaur
artworks.description: Painted in 1919 by the British artist Glyn Warren Philpot RA (1884–1937) and now in Glasgow Museums, this canvas gives the Greek seer Melampus a richly atmospheric Edwardian-classical treatment, pairing the youthful prophet with a centaur in a charged encounter of human and beast. The subject suits Melampus, who in legend understood the speech of animals — a gift won when serpents he had raised licked his ears clean — and who moved easily between the human and natural worlds as Greece's first mortal seer and healer. Philpot, celebrated for his sensuous handling of the male nude and his theatrical mythological compositions, here renders the meeting with a painterly warmth that places the ancient diviner squarely within early twentieth-century British Symbolist-classicism.
